intro: We use colours and clothes to describe people, to go shopping and to choose what to wear. Two points need care: the colour goes before the noun, and some clothes are always plural (trousers, jeans).
objectifs: Name colours and make them more exact (light blue, dark green, bright red).
Name common clothes and accessories, with British and American differences.
Use words that are always plural correctly: trousers, jeans, shorts, a pair of…
Choose the right verb: wear, carry, put on, take off, try on.

texte: A colour adjective goes before the noun and never takes an s: “a red car”, “red cars”. After “be”, it is alone: “The car is red.”
To be more exact: “light” (pale), “dark” (deep), “bright” (strong and shining): “light blue”, “dark green”. In speaking you can add “-ish”: “greenish” (more or less green).
The question is “What colour is it?”. Spelling: “colour”, “grey” in British English; “color”, “gray” in American English.
exemples: What colour is your car? — It's dark blue.
She's got a light grey coat.
sections.note: “Maroon” is a very dark red. For the colour of chocolate or wood, say “brown”.

texte: The word “clothes” is always plural and has no singular. For one thing, say “a piece of clothing” or use its name. “Cloth” (no e, no s) means material, or a piece of material for cleaning.

lignes: a shirt · a T-shirt · a blouse · a jumper · a jacket · a coat
a suit = jacket + trousers or skirt
a hat · a cap · a scarf · a belt · a tie · a bag

exemples: He's wearing a white shirt and a black tie.
Take a jumper. It's cold in the evening.
sections.note: In British English, “pants” means underwear! For the clothes on your legs, say “trousers” in the UK and “pants” in the USA and Canada.

texte: Clothes with two equal parts (two legs) are always plural in English: trousers, jeans, shorts, pyjamas (US pajamas), tights. The verb is plural: “My jeans are new.”
To count them, say “a pair of”: “a pair of jeans”, “two pairs of trousers”. Never say “a jean” or “a trouser”.
The same is true for “glasses” and “scissors”. We also count shoes and socks in pairs: “a pair of shoes”.
exemples: My new jeans are too long.
I need a pair of black trousers for work.

sections.titre: Wear, carry, put on, take off, try on
texte: “Wear” is for clothes, glasses or jewellery on your body. “Carry” is for things you hold and take with you (a bag, a child, a suitcase).
“Put on” = start to wear; “take off” = remove; “try on” = wear something in a shop to check it; “get dressed” = put on your clothes.
For what you are wearing today, use the present continuous; for a habit, use the present simple (lesson 9): “Today I'm wearing jeans, but I usually wear a suit.”

lignes: wear to check in a shop
Can I try on this dress?

exemples: Today I'm wearing jeans, but I usually wear a suit.
Put on your boots, it's raining.

formule: colour + clothes (a red dress) · a pair of + jeans / trousers / shoes · wear (on your body) ≠ carry (in your hand)
prononciation: “colour” /ˈkʌlə/: the first o sounds like the u in “but”.
“clothes” /kləʊðz/: one syllable. Many English speakers just say /kləʊz/, like “close”.
“shirt” /ʃɜːt/ and “skirt” /skɜːt/ have the same long vowel /ɜː/, like in “bird”.
“suit” /suːt/ rhymes with “boot”; you don't say the i.
“purple” /ˈpɜːpl/ and “orange” /ˈɒrɪndʒ/: stress on the first syllable; the end of “orange” sounds like “-rinj”.
erreurs: The colour goes before the noun.
I want a pair of jeans. / I want some jeans.
I carry a suit to work.
I wear a suit to work.
It's cold, put on your coat!
The action of starting to wear: “put on”.

dialogue.contexte: In Lyon, Chloé helps her friend Ibrahim choose clothes for a wedding.
lignes: What do I wear to the wedding on Saturday?
What about your dark blue suit and a white shirt?
Good idea. And a tie? I've got a red one and a green one.
“one” = tie, so we don't repeat it.
The red one. Red and dark blue look great together.
Colours as nouns: red, dark blue.
And shoes? My black shoes are old.
Let's go to the shops. You need a new pair.
OK. Can I wear my trainers to the party after?
Ha! Maybe. But take off your tie first!

mots: a piece of clothing with buttons and a collar
one piece of clothing for a woman, top and skirt together
She's got a long black skirt.
clothing for women that hangs from the waist
things you wear on your feet
a long, warm piece of clothing you wear outside
have clothes or glasses on your body
Put on your hat, it's sunny.
I need a new pair of jeans.
two things of the same kind used together

exercices.consigne: Complete with put on, wears, carries or take off.
items: He always ___ a suit at work.
She ___ her bag in her hand.
___ your shoes, please. The floor is clean.

exercices.consigne: Each sentence has one mistake. Write it correctly.
items: My trousers are grey. (US: My pants are gray.)
I've got two pairs of jeans.
Can I try these shoes on me?
Can I try on these shoes? / Can I try these shoes on?

exercices.consigne: In three or four sentences, describe what you are wearing today and what you usually wear for work or school. Give the colours.
items: Today I'm wearing blue jeans, a grey jumper and white trainers. At work I usually wear black trousers, a shirt and a dark jacket. My favourite colour is green, so I often wear a green scarf.

a_retenir: The colour goes before the noun and never changes: a red car, red cars. Question: What colour is it?
trousers, jeans, shorts, pyjamas, glasses: always plural; to count them: a pair of.
wear = on your body; carry = in your hands; put on = start to wear; take off = remove; try on = check in a shop.
UK / US: trousers / pants, jumper / sweater, trainers / sneakers, colour / color, grey / gray.
